title: J.P. Morgan Says Tesla’s Robotaxi Fleet Could Match Waymo’s Miles by Late 2027 With 18,000 Cars. The Number That Matters Is How Much Each Car Earns. - The Motley Fool
content: The robotaxi battle will be won and lost over the total cost of ownership per mile. J.P. Morgan analyst Rajat Gupta believes that Tesla's (TSLA -7.64%) robotaxi fleet could match Alphabet's (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%) Waymo fleet in cumulative autonomous miles by the end of 2027. Such an event would mark a milestone in Tesla's robotaxi development. Still, it's not the key metric that really matters, because this is a war likely to be won by a different and even more critical metric. It's such a key number that it will arguably determine Tesla's overall value. It's important to be clear about this number. Going back to the We, Robot event in 2024, Elon Musk outlined that the operating cost of a Cybercab is "probably going to be $0.20" per mile, with "The price of everything would be about $0.30 to $0.40 per mile," with a Cybercab cost of $30,000. However, these are Tesla's costs, so any individual buying a Cybercab to operate it as a robotaxi needs to factor in the $299-per-month full self-driving (FSD) subscription fee. Assuming a Cybercab is moderately run for 300,000 miles, it could rack up four years of subscriptions worth $14,352 in FSD costs. By "everything," Musk presumably means the fully loaded cost per mile, which includes Cybercab cost, energy cost, maintenance, cleaning, remote operations, and any other operational costs, in the TCO per-mile target of $0.30. This is where the battle over robotaxis will be won, because Tesla is highly likely to face competition from rivals developing low-cost electric vehicles (EVs) equipped with autonomous driving software. While its vision-only approach, leadership in EVs, scaling of Cybercab, and lead in the operational learning that will reduce TCO per mile give it a massive initial edge, it does not mean its robotaxi margins can't be eroded over time. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. To illustrate this, consider the following scenario: a Cybercab costing $30,000, with a useful life of 300,000 miles, compared with a low-cost EV robotaxi costing $20,000, with a useful life of 400,000 miles: The argument that bears often use against Tesla is that rivals could eat into its competitive advantage, but I think it's flawed. First, Tesla's vision-only approach implies lower structural hardware costs than the light detection and ranging (LiDAR) systems used by Waymo and others. Second, autonomous driving software is not free, and robotaxis need to be purposely built for it, both of which add costs for Tesla's rivals. Third, assuming that rivals could even get to $0.20-per-mile operating costs (or another figure close to where Tesla will get) assumes they can build scale and operational learning that Tesla is doing now. Finally, rivals could go for higher hardware costs (LiDAR plus licensed software) and more miles of robotaxi operation, but that would mean higher up-front costs, probably more maintenance costs, and robotaxis becoming obsolete more quickly. The good news is that Tesla's miles under robotaxi expansion mean it's learning to reduce TCO per mile before others can. That's a massive edge. Morgan Global Research has dropped a sobering message and reversed its "one and done" forecast on Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes. The Wall Street brokerage now calls for two additional increases, plus one in December, to tame persistent price pressures amid higher short-term borrowing costs. This means consumers and businesses can expect the interest rates on credit cards, student loans, and home-equity loans to rise through early 2027, and indirectly, mortgage rates and Treasury bond yields will also be influenced. As for investors, higher interest rates ripple through the stock market and investor portfolios via several core channels ranging from discounted cash flows and corporate borrowing costs to shifts in asset allocation. Back in September, I reported that J.P. Morgan economists called for only one additional 25-basis-point-rate hike by the central bank to curb sticky inflation fueled by the energy shocks from the Iran War and the supply-demand dynamic of artificial intelligence. But in a Nov. 19 client note obtained by Reuters, J.P. Morgan economists call for additional 25 basis-point-rate hikes at the Federal Open Market Committee's January and March meetings. "These ​hikes aren't to deliver a bad labor ​market, but to preserve credibility when they have ⁠no compelling narrative for a pause," J.P. ​Morgan strategists led by Michael Feroli said. This falls in line with what other Fed watchers and even what Fed officials are signaling: inflation is coming in way too hot. It's not only time for higher interest rates, but these hikes may in fact be overdue. "The labor market has not been a ​source of ​inflationary pressure, ⁠and yet inflation remains elevated," J.P. Morgan said, adding it expects modest, positive ​job growth next year. Brokerages BofA Global Research ⁠and Deutsche Bank also expect the central ​bank to increase the benchmark federal funds rate by 25 basis points at each of its next three meetings. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to dispense with forward guidance to markets after taking over the role in May has left the U.S. monetary policy path without an "overarching narrative," J.P. Morgan said. Forward guidance is a communication tool that the Fed used to signal the future path of monetary policy and interest rates to the public and financial markets in order to influence economic behavior and manage expectations. "Without a narrative as a pole star, policy ​is more likely to be reactive to incoming ​data," J.P. Morgan said. As I reported, minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee October meeting released Nov. 18, along with some very pointed public remarks from top Fed officials, show the U.S. central bank is becoming increasingly alarmed that price pressures are moving away from its 2% target, but there's a wide range of opinion within its ranks as to the best approach to lower price pressures. For investors, businesses and consumers, the emerging consensus signals that hopes for interest-rate relief in 2027 have all but evaporated. In fact, when the FOMC held its benchmark short-term interest rate steady at 3.75% to 4% in October with a divisive 10-2 vote, the minutes show several participants described the pause as a "close call." The CME Group's FedWatch Tool  projects roughly a 100% probability of a rate hike at the FOMC December meeting, a 48% probability of another in January 2027. The FedWatch Tool puts the probability of another 25-basis-point raise at the FOMC's March 2027 meeting at approximately 58%, suggesting traders increasingly expect additional monetary tightening early next year. At that point, traders expect the federal funds target range will have reached 4.25% to 4.50%. Related: Fed rate-cut hopes for 2027 take a stunning turn Four Fed Governors — Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Michael Barr, Lisa Cook and Christopher Waller — signaled decidedly hawkish tones in the past week, expressing that further tightening of policy was necessary to bring inflation back to its 2% target — a goal the central bank has missed for nearly six years. Waller doubled down on his comments earlier this month, saying that rising price pressures call for a jumbo 50-basis-point rate hike in December. "You might need to, like, shock people," he said in a Nov. 18 CNBC interview. Warsh has repeatedly said that the Fed is committed to its dual mandate: use interest rates and balance-sheet policy to keep prices stable and the labor market at full employment. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who will be a voting member of the FOMC in 2027, said in a Nov. 19 conference call with reporters that he will consider all options when policymakers meet again Dec. 8-9 to set interest rates. He did not push back against the possibility of a larger-than-usual interest rate increase. "The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy. I find it hard to…look at that any other way," Goolsbee said. "When you're getting major business investment, almost unprecedented levels of business investment, there's a high danger ​that the economy's capacity cannot handle that kind of a pig through the python." President Donald Trump has been criticizing the Fed for nearly a decade for not lowering interest rates to 1% or lower. He repeated his demands during a press conference Nov. 20, saying interest rates are high because the central bank's leaders are "too political." "Whenever we announce good numbers, they raise the rates. They do that for a reason,'' Trump said. "They do that to destroy the country." The growing prospect of another round of interest-rate increases keeps the independent central bank on a collision course with the Trump administration's calls for cheaper borrowing costs. For consumers, businesses and investors, the message from Wall Street is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: The era of waiting for lower interest rates may take longer than anyone wants. title: JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon to set ‘example’ after Healey’s bank tax hike - City AM
content: The boss of JP Morgan has warned he will seek to claw back the costs of John Healey’s bank tax hike after branding the move “unfair”. Jamie Dimon, regarded as one of the most influential figures in finance, said at an event in London on Thursday he would look to find ways to offset the Chancellor’s tax rise on the banking sector. Healey doubled the UK banking surcharge, which sits on top of corporation tax, to six per cent in his Budget for a 15 month period to strum up cash for an energy support package. Dimon said he plans to set “an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. He added that any move to offset the bank tax would be “more in sorrow” than anger, in comments first reported by the Financial Times. He did not specify what areas he would target to claw back costs. Three daily briefings with the key market moves and top business and political stories. JP Morgan quickly became one of the most vocal critics in the aftermath of Healey’s Budget. The lender said at the time that the tax increase “lacks principle” and hit out at Labour for singling out the banking sector. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has forecast the hike will raise around £1.5bn, with surcharge receipts pulling in £2.4bn in 2027. But the watchdog warned around £190m in receipts would be wiped out as some banks move profits out of the UK in response to the higher rate. It added that the total size of profits lost was “uncertain”. JP Morgan has laid out plans for a new mega-tower in Canary Wharf, which is expected to inject £10bn into the local economy and create 7,800 industry jobs. Dimon warned ahead of the Budget that any tax increases on the industry would have “adverse consequences”. The Wall Street giant also has a major campus in Bournemouth, where it employs some 5,300 staff processing more than $1tn of global transactions each day. There was speculation ahead of the Budget that the banking surcharge could be returned to its eight per cent rate. Share prices rallied following Healey’s announcement as the tax hike came in lower than expected. David Postings, the boss of trade body UK Finance, told a City audience this week: “It may be a smaller increase than some called for but a tax rise is still a tax rise, making an already uncompetitive regime even less competitive.” Subscribe to the City AM newsletter to have our top stories delivered directly to your inbox. title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks - The Guardian
content: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost. In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger. The boss of JP Morgan has warned that John Healey's bank tax raid will have consequences for Britain, as he vowed to set an "example" by finding ways to claw back the levy. In a veiled threat to the Government, Jamie Dimon said he wanted politicians to "understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties". Mr Dimon lashed out at the Chancellor after he temporarily doubled the surcharge on bank profits above £100m from 3pc to 6pc during his maiden Budget to provide "immediate support on energy bills". He said that any move to offset the bank tax would be "more in sorrow" than in anger, but failed to specify how he would claw back the costs, as first reported by the Financial Times. The Wall Street banking giant expects to pay between £100m to £150m because of Mr Healey's higher surcharge. Mr Dimon's latest comments will renew scrutiny of JP Morgan's proposals for a new £3bn headquarters in Canary Wharf. The bank has not suggested any reversal to the tower's development but it previously stressed that the project would depend on "a continuing positive business environment in the UK". The latest surcharge is levied in addition to the top rate of corporation tax, which now stands at 25pc. That means the biggest banks in Britain now face a total tax rate of 31pc – the highest level since at least 2015. Following the Budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimated that the higher tax rate will bring in an extra £1.5bn for the Treasury. However, it also claimed that the UK would lose roughly £190m of profits as a result of the tax rise. Mr Dimon has been among the staunchest critics of the policy, with the bank previously claiming that it has paid £5.5bn in bank taxes since 2011. In July, he said there would be "adverse consequences" if the Government targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes to help fund his spending plans. "I always thought it was wrong," he said. "We're a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there. title: JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard disclose cyberattacks targeting third-party vendors - KERN Radio
content: JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard disclosed Thursday that third-party service providers connected to their businesses were targeted in cyberattacks, potentially exposing limited customer information while leaving core banking and payment networks intact. The ransomware group known as n0n claimed responsibility for the intrusion and published stolen datasets online Thursday after an extortion deadline passed. None of the financial institutions identified the outside vendors targeted in the attack. The compromised records primarily consist of nonfinancial information, including customer names, email addresses, phone numbers and loyalty program engagement histories. According to a review of the leaked files, the Visa records centered on cardholders across Asia-Pacific markets such as Japan, Australia, Singapore and Hong Kong, whereas the Mastercard files involved benefit program enrollees in North America, the Middle East and Africa alongside a small number of employee email addresses. Separate leaks tied to JPMorgan Chase loyalty platforms reportedly affected roughly 16,000 individuals. All three companies emphasized that their internal infrastructure and payment processing systems were unaffected by the breach. A Mastercard spokesperson stated that the incident occurred “at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses — non-payments information — from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” adding that card usage remained uninterrupted. Similarly, a Visa spokesperson noted that “there is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected,” while confirming the breach originated with an Asia-Pacific vendor. JPMorgan Chase also addressed speculation linking the data theft to recent online banking disruptions, clarifying that the two events were separate. “There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” a bank spokesperson said, noting that the earlier outage stemmed from a software bug and that the bank would offer complimentary credit monitoring to affected customers where appropriate. Visa echoed that its own vendor breach was “unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week”. Cybersecurity researchers tracking n0n say the fast-growing extortion gang has claimed roughly 200 victims since emerging in September 2026 and relies heavily on artificial intelligence tools to identify software vulnerabilities. Although sensitive payment card numbers and security codes were not exposed in this incident, security analysts warn that leaked names, contact details and bank affiliations give scammers credible material to launch targeted phishing campaigns.

title: JP Morgan Chase — Cybersecurity Breach Exposed Following Major System Outage - The Korea Daily
content:
Major financial institution JP Morgan Chase suffered a cyberattack through an external vendor just three days after experiencing a massive computer system outage, resulting in the potential leakage of customer information. Alongside Chase, major global card networks Visa and Mastercard also reported exposure of customer data. According to Reuters, JP Morgan Chase stated that an external partner was targeted by a cyberattack, which may have compromised certain customer information. The hackers may have accessed marketing materials containing customer names and email addresses. The hacking group ‘n0n’ claimed on the 16th that it had secured customer information from Chase, Visa, and Mastercard, subsequently releasing related data. The data verified by Reuters contained email addresses of approximately 16,000 Chase customers and 124 employees, along with some phone numbers and postal codes, though the authenticity of the leaked data has not been independently verified. Some of the exposed data is reportedly linked to Chase’s invitation-only credit card program targeting customers with assets exceeding $10 million. Visa and Mastercard also experienced breaches through external vendors. Visa noted that its Asia-Pacific regional partner was targeted, with leaked data including email addresses and phone numbers of customers in South Korea, Japan, Taiwan, and Hong Kong. However, Visa emphasized that its internal network and payment information, such as card numbers, remained unaffected. Mastercard explained that email addresses of certain customers enrolled in specific benefit programs were exposed, but transaction networks and card usage were not impacted. Previously on the 16th, software errors caused transaction delays and login failures for major bank customers, including Chase, Bank of America (BOA), and Wells Fargo. Bank officials stated that the earlier system outage and this recent hacking incident are unrelated. Concerns over personal data leaks extend beyond the financial sector. In California, potential exposure of personal information for 7 million current and former public school students has embroiled educational authorities in a class-action lawsuit. According to the California Post, Dane Wilson, a California public school graduate, filed a class-action lawsuit on the 2nd against the California Department of Education and testing agency ETS. The complaint alleges that hackers infiltrated ETS computer networks between May and September of last year, potentially accessing students’ names, dates of birth, home addresses, disability records, and test scores. Potentially affected individuals include students who attended or graduated from California public schools since 2023. The plaintiffs accused educational authorities and ETS of neglecting their duty to protect personal information, demanding improved security systems and compensation. Consumer and community banking, the corporate and markets bank, commercial banking and asset and wealth management each contributed, and the diversity of those engines helped the firm post firm results even as parts of the lending landscape softened. Management described the core businesses as strengthening, a framing the market welcomed. Financials have steadied into year-end even as the louder drama has played out in technology. While the artificial-intelligence trade swung and chip names seesawed, the banking group drew a different kind of attention, anchored by earnings season and by the debate over credit quality. That steadier tone has made the sector a point of relative calm during a choppy stretch for the broad market. JPMorgan Chase operates one of the most diversified franchises in global finance, spanning consumer and community banking, a sprawling corporate and markets bank, commercial banking and asset and wealth management. That breadth lets the firm serve households, small businesses, large corporations, governments and institutions from a single platform, and it is the reason the bank is treated as a bellwether for the entire sector. JPMorgan Chase sits at the apex of the US banking system, combining a dominant consumer franchise with a top-tier markets and advisory arm and a large asset-and-wealth business. That blend smooths the cyclicality of any single unit, so when lending cools, trading or advisory can pick up the slack, and vice versa. The latest quarter reinforced that balance, with several units contributing to a firm result. The standout development was the strength across the firm's core units, with revenue rising and the consumer, markets and advisory engines each contributing. That breadth matters because it shows the franchise is not leaning on any single line, a quality the market prizes when parts of the lending landscape show strain. Heading into year-end, the operational focus turns to credit quality, deposit trends and the trajectory of capital-markets activity. Banks of this scale watch loan performance closely as the economy navigates a shifting rate environment, and the firm's ability to manage credit through the cycle is one of the reasons it is regarded as a steady hand in uncertain stretches. Banks face a familiar set of challenges. The direction of rates shapes lending margins, credit quality can shift as the economy turns, and competition from both established peers and newer financial-technology entrants keeps pressure on fees and deposits. The swelling private-credit market adds a fresh dimension, drawing lending activity into less-regulated channels that the market is still learning to gauge. JPMorgan Chase competes with the other large money-center banks, with regional lenders, with global markets-and-advisory houses and increasingly with asset managers and financial-technology firms pressing into payments, lending and wealth. What distinguishes its position is the sheer breadth of its franchise, which lets it meet customers across nearly every financial need from a single, deeply resourced platform. Because of its size and its central role in the financial system, JPMorgan Chase functions as a barometer for the health of banking and the broader economy.
